Do not stop after writing a stub, a plan, or a single command. Keep working until you have actually exercised the code or produced the requested result, then report what real execution returned.

Reporting a blocker honestly is always better than inventing a result.

Independent reads, searches, web fetches, and read-only commands should be batched into the same assistant turn — the runtime executes independent calls concurrently, and batching avoids resending the whole conversation on every extra round-trip.
Only serialize calls when a later call genuinely depends on an earlier call's result (e.g. you must read a file before you can patch it). When in doubt and the calls are independent, batch them.

Specifically: do not record PR numbers, issue numbers, commit SHAs, 'fixed bug X', 'submitted PR Y', 'Phase N done', file counts, or any artifact that will be stale in 7 days. If a fact will be stale in a week, it does not belong in memory. If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.

'Project uses pytest with xdist' ✓ — 'Run tests with pytest -n 4' ✗. Imperative phrasing gets re-read as a directive in later sessions and can cause repeated work or override the user's current request. Procedures and workflows belong in skills, not memory. When the user references something from a past conversation or you suspect relevant cross-session context exists, use session_search to recall it before asking them to repeat themselves. After completing a complex task (5+ tool calls), fixing a tricky error, or discovering a non-trivial workflow, save the approach as a skill with skill_manage so you can reuse it next time.
When using a skill and finding it outdated, incomplete, or wrong, patch it immediately with skill_manage(action='patch') — don't wait to be asked. Skills that aren't maintained become liabilities.

27|## Searching Papers

37|### Clean output (parse XML to readable format)
38|
39|```bash
40|curl -s "https://export.arxiv.org/api/query?search_query=all:GRPO+reinforcement+learning&max_results=5&sortBy=submittedDate&sortOrder=descending" | python3 -c "
41|import sys, xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
42|ns = {'a': 'http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom'}
43|root = ET.parse(sys.stdin).getroot()
44|for i, entry in enumerate(root.findall('a:entry', ns)):
45|    title = entry.find('a:title', ns).text.strip().replace('\n', ' ')
46|    arxiv_id = entry.find('a:id', ns).text.strip().split('/abs/')[-1]
47|    published = entry.find('a:published', ns).text[:10]
48|    authors = ', '.join(a.find('a:name', ns).text for a in entry.findall('a:author', ns))
49|    summary = entry.find('a:summary', ns).text.strip()[:200]
50|    cats = ', '.join(c.get('term') for c in entry.findall('a:category', ns))
51|    print(f'{i+1}. [{arxiv_id}] {title}')
52|    print(f'   Authors: {authors}')
53|    print(f'   Published: {published} | Categories: {cats}')

127|authors = ' and '.join(a.find('a:name', ns).text for a in entry.findall('a:author', ns))
128|year = entry.find('a:published', ns).text[:4]
129|raw_id = entry.find('a:id', ns).text.strip().split('/abs/')[-1]
130|cat = entry.find('arxiv:primary_category', ns)

132|last_name = entry.find('a:author', ns).find('a:name', ns).text.split()[-1]
133|print(f'@article{{{last_name}{year}_{raw_id.replace(\".\", \"\")},')

136|print(f'  year      = {{{year}}},')
137|print(f'  eprint    = {{{raw_id}}},')
138|print(f'  archivePrefix = {{arXiv}},')
139|print(f'  primaryClass  = {{{primary}}},')

244|## Complete Research Workflow
245|
246|1. **Discover**: `python scripts/search_arxiv.py "your topic" --sort date --max 10`
247|2. **Assess impact**: `curl -s "https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/arXiv:ID?fields=citationCount,influentialCitationCount"`
248|3. **Read abstract**: `web_extract(urls=["https://arxiv.org/abs/ID"])`
249|4. **Read full paper**: `web_extract(urls=["https://arxiv.org/pdf/ID"])`
250|5. **Find related work**: `curl -s "https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/arXiv:ID/references?fields=title,citationCount&limit=20"`
251|6. **Get recommendations**: POST to Semantic Scholar recommendations endpoint
252|7. **Track authors**: `curl -s "https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/author/search?query=NAME"`

254|## Rate Limits
255|
256|| API | Rate | Auth |
257||-----|------|------|
258|| arXiv | ~1 req / 3 seconds | None needed |
259|| Semantic Scholar | 1 req / second | None (100/sec with API key) |

261|## Notes
262|
263|- arXiv returns Atom XML — use the helper script or parsing snippet for clean output
264|- Semantic Scholar returns JSON — pipe through `python3 -m json.tool` for readability
265|- arXiv IDs: old format (`hep-th/0601001`) vs new (`2402.03300`)
266|- PDF: `https://arxiv.org/pdf/{id}` — Abstract: `https://arxiv.org/abs/{id}`
267|- HTML (when available): `https://arxiv.org/html/{id}`
268|- For local PDF processing, see the `ocr-and-documents` skill
269|
270|## ID Versioning
271|
272|- `arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762` always resolves to the **latest** version
273|- `arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762v1` points to a **specific** immutable version
274|- When generating citations, preserve the version suffix you actually read to prevent citation drift (a later version may substantially change content)
275|- The API `<id>` field returns the versioned URL (e.g., `http://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762v7`)
276|
277|## Withdrawn Papers
278|
279|Papers can be withdrawn after submission. When this happens:
280|- The `<summary>` field contains a withdrawal notice (look for "withdrawn" or "retracted")
281|- Metadata fields may be incomplete
282|- Always check the summary before treating a result as a valid paper

ABSTRACT: This feature article provides an overview of the theoretical foundations for coVariance neural networks (VNNs), i.e., graph neural networks (GNNs) operating on covariance matrices as graphs. Covariance matrices are ubiquitous across domains, and hence, the deployment of GNNs often leverages graphs of pairwise statistical dependencies. Existing theoretical contributions on GNNs consider abstract graph representations and cannot accommodate the data-driven nuances associated with covariance matrices. This tutorial brings into focus various novel theoretical insights via mathematical analyses of VNNs that have broad signal processing implications, including: (i) a conceptual equivalence between VNNs and principal component analysis (PCA)-based information processing; (ii) refined stability bounds on predictive outcomes in the presence of finite sample-induced covariance matrix perturbations; and (iii) refined characterization of transferability of VNNs across multiscale datasets. The theoretical insights discussed herein provide the underlying principles and justification towards adopting VNNs over workhorse PCA-based learning pipelines, in applications where covariance matrices are useful descriptors of data structure. We also convey how impact of these foundational advances permeates to \textit{principled} designs and applications of learning methods across broad domains where covariance matrices emerge. Notably, we elucidate the conceptual insights facilitated by VNNs to the specific task of characterizing brain age gap for neurodegenerative conditions using neuroimaging datasets, a timely problem in computational neuroscience. Broader impacts to other application domains are discussed as well.

TITLE: Likelihood-free inference with nuisance parameters through normalizing flows
AUTHORS: Phil Assheton
DATE: 2026-09-09
CATEGORIES: stat.ME, cs.LG, stat.ML
ABSTRACT: We present a simple decomposition of a neural-network-based normalizing flow that naturally uncovers a pivotal statistic (or something close) in the presence of nuisance parameters, based only on a sample generator from the distribution of interest. We show that the statistic is near-pivotal in the sense of minimum average KL-divergence of its $p$-values versus uniform and we argue that it can be expected to have good power when the dimension of the statistic equals the dimension of the parameter. It is able to incorporate prior knowledge about group invariances such as translation and scale. 105|def _collect_delegate_child_ids(conn, parent_ids: List[str]) -> List[str]:

336|def _apply_macos_checkpoint_barrier(conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> None:
337|    """Enable ``PRAGMA checkpoint_fullfsync`` on macOS (no-op elsewhere).
338|
339|    On Darwin, ``synchronous=FULL`` (the WAL default) issues a plain
340|    ``fsync()``, which Apple documents does *not* guarantee that data
341|    has reached stable storage or that writes are not reordered — see
342|    the ``fsync(2)`` man page.  SQLite's WAL corruption-safety guarantee
343|    assumes the OS honors the fsync write barrier; macOS does not unless
344|    the app uses ``F_FULLFSYNC``.
345|
346|    During a launchd *system* shutdown/reboot the OS page cache is
347|    dropped (effectively a power-loss event for in-flight pages), so a
348|    WAL checkpoint whose ``fsync()`` "reported" durable may never have
349|    hit the platter — corrupting ``state.db`` with a malformed image.
350|    This is the trigger in issue #30636 ("SIGTERM during launchd
351|    shutdown under high load"), distinct from a plain in-session kill
352|    (which the page cache survives and SQLite recovers from).
353|
354|    ``checkpoint_fullfsync=1`` forces an ``F_FULLFSYNC`` barrier only at
355|    checkpoint boundaries — where WAL frames land in the main DB — so the
356|    cost amortizes to roughly +0.1 ms/commit (vs ~+4 ms for the broader
357|    ``fullfsync=1`` that flushes on every commit's WAL sync).  Guarded by
358|    ``sys.platform == "darwin"`` because ``F_FULLFSYNC`` is macOS-only;
359|    on other platforms the PRAGMA is a no-op, so we skip it entirely.
360|
361|    Best-effort: never raises.
362|    """

371|def _enforce_macos_synchronous_full(conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> None:

375|    which Apple's fsync(2) man page explicitly states does *not* guarantee
376|    data-on-platter or write-ordering. During a WAL checkpoint race with
377|    process termination (e.g., launchd shutdown), this can leave the main
378|    DB with half-written btree pages → ``btreeInitPage error 11``.
379|
380|    WAL mode's durability guarantee assumes the OS honors fsync barriers;
381|    macOS does not unless we explicitly set ``synchronous=FULL``, which issues
382|    a real ``fsync()`` on every transaction commit.  The ``F_FULLFSYNC``
383|    barrier at checkpoint boundaries is handled separately by
384|    :func:`_apply_macos_checkpoint_barrier`.
385|

389|    synchronous mode, even if a prior connection set ``synchronous=NORMAL``.
390|
391|    Best-effort: never raises.
392|    """

401|def apply_wal_with_fallback(
402|    conn: sqlite3.Connection,
403|    *,
404|    db_label: str = "state.db",
405|) -> str:
406|    """Set ``journal_mode=WAL`` on ``conn``, falling back to DELETE on failure.
407|

409|
410|    On WAL-incompatible filesystems (NFS, SMB, some FUSE), SQLite raises
411|    ``OperationalError("locking protocol")`` when setting WAL.  We fall
412|    back to DELETE mode — the pre-WAL default, which works on NFS — and
413|    log one WARNING explaining why.
414|
415|    The WARNING is deduplicated per ``db_label``: repeated connections
416|    to the same underlying DB (e.g. kanban_db.connect() which is called
417|    on every kanban operation) log once per process, not once per call.
418|    Different db_labels log independently, so state.db and kanban.db
419|    each get one warning on the same NFS mount.
420|
421|    Shared by :class:`SessionDB` and ``hermes_cli.kanban_db.connect`` so
422|    both databases get identical fallback behavior.

424|    Never downgrades to DELETE if the on-disk DB header reports WAL — see _on_disk_journal_mode.
425|    """
426|    # Read-only probe — no flock, no checkpoint, no WAL/SHM unlink.
427|    # Skipping the set-pragma prevents WAL-init from unlinking files other connections hold open.
428|    try:
429|        current_mode = conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode").fetchone()
430|        if current_mode and current_mode[0] == "wal":
431|            _apply_macos_checkpoint_barrier(conn)
432|            _enforce_macos_synchronous_full(conn)
433|            return "wal"
434|    except sqlite3.OperationalError:
435|        pass
436|
437|    try:
438|        conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
439|        _apply_macos_checkpoint_barrier(conn)
440|        _enforce_macos_synchronous_full(conn)
441|        return "wal"
442|    except sqlite3.OperationalError as exc:
443|        msg = str(exc).lower()
444|        if not any(marker in msg for marker in _WAL_INCOMPAT_MARKERS):
445|            # Unrelated OperationalError — don't silently swallow.
446|            raise
447|        # Don't downgrade if another process already set WAL on disk.
448|        existing = _on_disk_journal_mode(conn)
449|        if existing == "wal":
450|            raise
451|        _log_wal_fallback_once(db_label, exc)
452|        conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE")
453|        return "delete"

456|def _log_wal_fallback_once(db_label: str, exc: Exception) -> None:
457|    """Log a single WARNING per (process, db_label) about WAL fallback.

459|    Without this dedup, NFS users running kanban (which opens a fresh
460|    connection on every operation — see hermes_cli/kanban_db.py) would

465|            return

469|        "falling back to journal_mode=DELETE (slower rollback-journal "
470|        "mode; reduces concurrency but works on NFS/SMB/FUSE). See "
471|        "https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html for details. This warning "
472|        "fires once per process per database.",

172|class StreamingContextScrubber:
173|    """Stateful scrubber for streaming text that may contain split memory-context spans.
174|
175|    The one-shot ``sanitize_context`` regex cannot survive chunk boundaries:
176|    a ``<memory-context>`` opened in one delta and closed in a later delta
177|    leaks its payload to the UI because the non-greedy block regex needs
178|    both tags in one string.  This scrubber runs a small state machine
179|    across deltas, holding back partial-tag tails and discarding
180|    everything inside a span (including the system-note line).
181|
182|    Usage::
183|
184|        scrubber = StreamingContextScrubber()
185|        for delta in stream:
186|            visible = scrubber.feed(delta)
187|            if visible:
188|                emit(visible)
189|        trailing = scrubber.flush()  # at end of stream
190|        if trailing:
191|            emit(trailing)

193|    The scrubber is re-entrant per agent instance.  Callers building new
194|    top-level responses (new turn) should create a fresh scrubber or call
195|    ``reset()``.
196|    """
197|
198|    _OPEN_TAG = "<memory-context>"
199|    _CLOSE_TAG = "</memory-context>"
200|
201|    def __init__(self) -> None:
202|        self._in_span: bool = False
203|        self._buf: str = ""
204|        self._at_block_boundary: bool = True
205|
206|    def reset(self) -> None:
207|        self._in_span = False
208|        self._buf = ""
209|        self._at_block_boundary = True
210|
211|    def feed(self, text: str) -> str:
212|        """Return the visible portion of ``text`` after scrubbing.
213|
214|        Any trailing fragment that could be the start of an open/close tag
215|        is held back in the internal buffer and surfaced on the next
216|        ``feed()`` call or discarded/emitted by ``flush()``.
217|        """
218|        if not text:
219|            return ""
220|        buf = self._buf + text
221|        self._buf = ""
222|        out: list[str] = []
223|
224|        while buf:
225|            if self._in_span:
226|                idx = buf.lower().find(self._CLOSE_TAG)
227|                if idx == -1:
228|                    # Hold back a potential partial close tag; drop the rest
229|                    held = self._max_partial_suffix(buf, self._CLOSE_TAG)
230|                    self._buf = buf[-held:] if held else ""
231|                    return "".join(out)
232|                # Found close — skip span content + tag, continue
233|                buf = buf[idx + len(self._CLOSE_TAG):]
234|                self._in_span = False
235|            else:
236|                idx = self._find_boundary_open_tag(buf)
237|                if idx == -1:

{"content": "1|"""Abstract base class for pluggable memory providers.
2|
3|Memory providers give the agent persistent recall across sessions.
4|The MemoryManager enforces a one-external-provider limit to prevent
5|tool schema bloat and conflicting memory backends.
6|
7|External providers (Honcho, Hindsight, Mem0, etc.) are registered
8|and managed via MemoryManager. Only one external provider runs at a
9|time.
10|
11|Registration:
12|  Plugins ship in plugins/memory/<name>/ and are activated via
13|  the memory.provider config key.
14|
15|Lifecycle (called by MemoryManager, wired in run_agent.py):
16|  initialize()          — connect, create resources, warm up
17|  system_prompt_block()  — static text for the system prompt
18|  prefetch(query)        — background recall before each turn
19|  sync_turn(user, asst)  — async write after each turn
20|  get_tool_schemas()     — tool schemas to expose to the model
21|  handle_tool_call()     — dispatch a tool call
22|  shutdown()             — clean exit
23|
24|Optional hooks (override to opt in):
25|  on_turn_start(turn, message, **kwargs) — per-turn tick with runtime context
26|  on_session_end(messages)               — end-of-session extraction
27|  on_session_switch(new_session_id, **kwargs) — mid-process session_id rotation
28|  on_pre_compress(messages) -> str       — extract before context compression

63|        """Initialize for a session.
64|
65|        Called once at agent startup. May create resources (banks, tables),
66|        establish connections, start background threads, etc.
67|
68|        kwargs always include:
69|          - hermes_home (str): The active HERMES_HOME directory path. Use this
70|            for profile-scoped storage instead of hardcoding ``~/.hermes``.
71|          - platform (str): "cli", "telegram", "discord", "cron", etc.
72|
73|        kwargs may also include:
74|          - agent_context (str): "primary", "subagent", "cron", or "flush".
75|            Providers should skip writes for non-primary contexts (cron system
76|            prompts would corrupt user representations).
77|          - agent_identity (str): Profile name (e.g. "coder"). Use for
78|            per-profile provider identity scoping.
79|          - agent_workspace (str): Shared workspace name (e.g. "hermes").
80|          - parent_session_id (str): For subagents, the parent's session_id.
81|          - user_id (str): Platform user identifier (gateway sessions).
82|          - user_id_alt (str): Optional alternate stable platform user identifier.
83|        """

86|        """Return text to include in the system prompt.
87|
88|        Called during system prompt assembly. Return empty string to skip.
89|        This is for STATIC provider info (instructions, status). Prefetched
90|        recall context is injected separately via prefetch().
91|        """
92|        return ""
93|
94|    def prefetch(self, query: str, *, session_id: str = "") -> str:
95|        """Recall relevant context for the upcoming turn.
96|
97|        Called before each API call. Return formatted text to inject as
98|        context, or empty string if nothing relevant. Implementations
99|        should be fast — use background threads for the actual recall
100|        and return cached results here.
101|
102|        session_id is provided for providers serving concurrent sessions
103|        (gateway group chats, cached agents). Providers that don't need
104|        per-session scoping can ignore it.
105|        """
106|        return ""
107|
108|    def queue_prefetch(self, query: str, *, session_id: str = "") -> None:
109|        """Queue a background recall for the NEXT turn.
110|
111|        Called after each turn completes. The result will be consumed
112|        by prefetch() on the next turn. Default is no-op — providers
113|        that do background prefetching should override this.
114|        """
115|
116|    def sync_turn(
117|        self,
118|        user_content: str,
119|        assistant_content: str,
120|        *,
121|        session_id: str = "",
122|        messages: Optional[List[Dict[str, Any]]] = None,
123|    ) -> None:
124|        """Persist a completed turn to the backend.
125|
126|        Called after each turn. Should be non-blocking — queue for
127|        background processing if the backend has latency.
128|
129|        ``messages`` is the OpenAI-style conversation message list as of the
130|        completed turn, including any assistant tool calls and tool results.
131|        Providers that do not need raw turn context can ignore it.
132|        """
133|
134|    @abstractmethod
135|    def get_tool_schemas(self) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
136|        """Return tool schemas this provider exposes.
137|
138|        Each schema follows the OpenAI function calling format:
139|        {"name": "...", "description": "...", "parameters": {...}}
140|
141|        Return empty list if this provider has no tools (context-only).
142|        """
143|
144|    def handle_tool_call(self, tool_name: str, args: Dict[str, Any], **kwargs) -> str:
145|        """Handle a tool call for one of this provider's tools.
146|
147|        Must return a JSON string (the tool result).
148|        Only called for tool names returned by get_tool_schemas().
149|        """
150|        raise NotImplementedError(f"Provider {self.name} does not handle tool {tool_name}")
151|
152|    def shutdown(self) -> None:
153|        """Clean shutdown — flush queues, close connections."""

158|        """Called at the start of each turn with the user message.
159|
160|        Use for turn-counting, scope management, periodic maintenance.
161|
162|        kwargs may include: remaining_tokens, model, platform, tool_count.
163|        Providers use what they need; extras are ignored.
164|        """
165|
166|    def on_session_end(self, messages: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> None:
167|        """Called when a session ends (explicit exit or timeout).
168|
169|        Use for end-of-session fact extraction, summarization, etc.
170|        messages is the full conversation history.
171|
172|        NOT called after every turn — only at actual session boundaries
173|        (CLI exit, /reset, gateway session expiry).
174|        """
175|

177|        self,
178|        new_session_id: str,
179|        *,
180|        parent_session_id: str = "",
181|        reset: bool = False,

{"content": "1|---
2|name: llm-wiki
3|description: "Karpathy's LLM Wiki: build/query interlinked markdown KB."
4|version: 2.1.0
5|author: Hermes Agent
6|license: MIT
7|platforms: [linux, macos, windows]
8|metadata:
9|  hermes:
10|    tags: [wiki, knowledge-base, research, notes, markdown, rag-alternative]
11|    category: research
12|    related_skills: [obsidian, arxiv]
13|---
14|
15|# Karpathy's LLM Wiki
16|
17|Build and maintain a persistent, compounding knowledge base as interlinked markdown files.
18|Based on [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f).
19|
20|Unlike traditional RAG (which rediscovers knowledge from scratch per query), the wiki
21|compiles knowledge once and keeps it current. Cross-references are already there.
22|Contradictions have already been flagged. Synthesis reflects everything ingested.
23|
24|**Division of labor:** The human curates sources and directs analysis. The agent
25|summarizes, cross-references, files, and maintains consistency.
26|
27|## When This Skill Activates
28|
29|Use this skill when the user:
30|- Asks to create, build, or start a wiki or knowledge base
31|- Asks to ingest, add, or process a source into their wiki
32|- Asks a question and an existing wiki is present at the configured path
33|- Asks to lint, audit, or health-check their wiki
34|- References their wiki, knowledge base, or "notes" in a research context
35|
36|## Wiki Location
37|
38|**Location:** Set via `WIKI_PATH` environment variable (e.g. in `~/.hermes/.env`).
39|
40|If unset, defaults to `~/wiki`.
41|
42|```bash
43|WIKI="${WIKI_PATH:-$HOME/wiki}"
44|```
45|
46|The wiki is just a directory of markdown files — open it in Obsidian, VS Code, or
47|any editor. No database, no special tooling required.
48|
49|## Architecture: Three Layers
50|
51|```
52|wiki/
53|├── SCHEMA.md           # Conventions, structure rules, domain config
54|├── index.md            # Sectioned content catalog with one-line summaries
55|├── log.md              # Chronological action log (append-only, rotated yearly)
56|├── raw/                # Layer 1: Immutable source material
57|│   ├── articles/       # Web articles, clippings
58|│   ├── papers/         # PDFs, arxiv papers
59|│   ├── transcripts/    # Meeting notes, interviews
60|│   └── assets/         # Images, diagrams referenced by sources
61|├── entities/           # Layer 2: Entity pages (people, orgs, products, models)
62|├── concepts/           # Layer 2: Concept/topic pages
63|├── comparisons/        # Layer 2: Side-by-side analyses
64|└── queries/            # Layer 2: Filed query results worth keeping
65|```
66|
67|**Layer 1 — Raw Sources:** Immutable. The agent reads but never modifies these.
68|**Layer 2 — The Wiki:** Agent-owned markdown files. Created, updated, and
69|cross-referenced by the agent.
70|**Layer 3 — The Schema:** `SCHEMA.md` defines structure, conventions, and tag taxonomy.
71|
72|## Resuming an Existing Wiki (CRITICAL — do this every session)
73|
74|When the user has an existing wiki, **always orient yourself before doing anything**:
75|
76|① **Read `SCHEMA.md`** — understand the domain, conventions, and tag taxonomy.
77|② **Read `index.md`** — learn what pages exist and their summaries.
78|③ **Scan recent `log.md`** — read the last 20-30 entries to understand recent activity.
79|
80|```bash
81|WIKI="${WIKI_PATH:-$HOME/wiki}"
82|# Orientation reads at session start
83|read_file "$WIKI/SCHEMA.md"
84|read_file "$WIKI/index.md"
85|read_file "$WIKI/log.md" offset=<last 30 lines>
86|```
87|
88|Only after orientation should you ingest, query, or lint. This prevents:
89|- Creating duplicate pages for entities that already exist
90|- Missing cross-references to existing content
91|- Contradicting the schema's conventions
92|- Repeating work already logged
93|
94|For large wikis (100+ pages), also run a quick `search_files` for the topic
95|at hand before creating anything new.
96|
97|## Initializing a New Wiki
98|
99|When the user asks to create or start a wiki:
100|
101|1. Determine the wiki path (from `$WIKI_PATH` env var, or ask the user; default `~/wiki`)
102|2. Create the directory structure above
103|3. Ask the user what domain the wiki covers — be specific
104|4. Write `SCHEMA.md` customized to the domain (see template below)
105|5. Write initial `index.md` with sectioned header
106|6. Write initial `log.md` with creation entry
107|7. Confirm the wiki is ready and suggest first sources to ingest
108|
109|### SCHEMA.md Template
110|
111|Adapt to the user's domain. The schema constrains agent behavior and ensures consistency:
112|
113|```markdown
114|# Wiki Schema
115|
116|## Domain
117|[What this wiki covers — e.g., "AI/ML research", "personal health", "startup intelligence"]
118|
119|## Conventions
120|- File names: lowercase, hyphens, no spaces (e.g., `transformer-architecture.md`)
121|- Every wiki page starts with YAML frontmatter (see below)
122|- Use `[[wikilinks]]` to link between pages (minimum 2 outbound links per page)
123|- When updating a page, always bump the `updated` date
124|- Every new page must be added to `index.md` under the correct section
125|- Every action must be appended to `log.md`
126|- **Provenance markers:** On pages that synthesize 3+ sources, append `^[raw/articles/source-file.md]`
127|  at the end of paragraphs whose claims come from a specific source. This lets a reader trace each
128|  claim back without re-reading the whole raw file. Optional on single-source pages where the
129|  `sources:` frontmatter is enough.
130|
131|## Frontmatter
132|  ```yaml
133|  ---
134|  title: Page Title
135|  created: YYYY-MM-DD
136|  updated: YYYY-MM-DD
137|  type: entity | concept | comparison | query | summary
138|  tags: [from taxonomy below]
139|  sources: [raw/articles/source-name.md]
140|  # Optional quality signals:
141|  confidence: high | medium | low        # how well-supported the claims are
142|  contested: true                        # set when the page has unresolved contradictions
143|  contradictions: [other-page-slug]      # pages this one conflicts with
144|  ---
145|  ```
146|
147|`confidence` and `contested` are optional but recommended for opinion-heavy or fast-moving
148|topics. Lint surfaces `contested: true` and `confidence: low` pages for review so weak claims
149|don't silently harden into accepted wiki fact.
150|
151|### raw/ Frontmatter
152|
153|Raw sources ALSO get a small frontmatter block so re-ingests can detect drift:
154|
155|```yaml
156|---
157|source_url: https://example.com/article   # original URL, if applicable
158|ingested: YYYY-MM-DD
159|sha256: <hex digest of the raw content below the frontmatter>
160|---
161|```
162|
163|The `sha256:` lets a future re-ingest of the same URL skip processing when content is unchanged,
164|and flag drift when it has changed. Compute over the body only (everything after the closing
165|`---`), not the frontmatter itself.
166|
167|## Tag Taxonomy
168|[Define 10-20 top-level tags for the domain. Add new tags here BEFORE using them.]
169|
170|Example for AI/ML:
171|- Models: model, architecture, benchmark, training
172|- People/Orgs: person, company, lab, open-source
173|- Techniques: optimization, fine-tuning, inference, alignment, data
174|- Meta: comparison, timeline, controversy, prediction
175|
176|Rule: every tag on a page must appear in this taxonomy. If a new tag is needed,
177|add it here first, then use it. This prevents tag sprawl.
178|
179|## Page Thresholds
180|- **Create a page** when an entity/concept appears in 2+ sources OR is central to one source
181|- **Add to existing page** when a source mentions something already covered
182|- **DON'T create a page** for passing mentions, minor details, or things outside the domain
183|- **Split a page** when it exceeds ~200 lines — break into sub-topics with cross-links
184|- **Archive a page** when its content is fully superseded — move to `_archive/`, remove from index
185|
186|## Entity Pages
187|One page per notable entity. Include:
188|- Overview / what it is
189|- Key facts and dates
190|- Relationships to other entities ([[wikilinks]])
191|- Source references
192|
193|## Concept Pages
194|One page per concept or topic. Include:
195|- Definition / explanation
196|- Current state of knowledge
197|- Open questions or debates
198|- Related concepts ([[wikilinks]])
199|
200|## Comparison Pages
201|Side-by-side analyses. Include:
202|- What is being compared and why
203|- Dimensions of comparison (table format preferred)
204|- Verdict or synthesis
205|- Sources
206|
207|## Update Policy
208|When new information conflicts with existing content:
209|1. Check the dates — newer sources generally supersede older ones
210|2. If genuinely contradictory, note both positions with dates and sources
211|3. Mark the contradiction in frontmatter: `contradictions: [page-name]`
212|4. Flag for user review in the lint report
213|```
214|
215|### index.md Template

## Hermes Memory Management — Deep Dive

### Storage Architecture

**1. Primary Persistent Store**: SQLite database at `/root/.hermes/profiles/biraj/state.db`
- **WAL mode** (Write-Ahead Logging) for concurrent readers + single writer (falls back to DELETE on incompatible filesystems)
- **FTS5 full-text search** virtual tables (`messages_fts`, `messages_fts_trigram`) for efficient text search across all session messages
- Schema version 22 — tracks migrations and schema integrity

**2. Built-in Plain-Text Memory Files** (always active, no external provider needed):
- `memories/MEMORY.md` — Working memory notes (user-scoped facts, observations, standing rules). Currently at 4% of 2,200-char budget (1 entry).
- `memories/USER.md` — User profile (name, role, organization, preferences). At 20% of 1,375-char budget (3 fields).
- Both written during profile init by `init_employee.py` using `AGENT_STEA003_AI_ML_SOFTWARE_ENGINEER` template.

**3. Session Data in SQLite** (`state.db`):
| Table | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `messages` | Full conversation history + metadata (tokens, roles, tool calls, timestamps) |
| `sessions` | Session metadata (model, config, parent/child relationships, compression flags) |
| `session_model_usage` | Per-session model/API usage stats |
| `messages_fts` / `messages_fts_trigram` | FTS5 indexes for text search |
| `compression_locks`, `delivery_obligations` | Internal housekeeping |

### Memory Lifecycle Flow

1. **On Session Start** → `MemoryManager.__init__()` loads built-in provider + (optional) one external provider
2. **`prefetch_all(query)`** — Before each turn, strips skill scaffolding, queries all providers, merges context
   - Built-in provider returns MEMORY.md + USER.md content wrapped in `<memory-context>` fence
   - External providers (honcho/hindsight/mem0, etc.) run in background threads with timeout guards
3. **`sync_all(user_msg, assistant_msg)`** — After each turn, writes to providers via background worker (single-threaded daemon executor)
   - Never blocks the main turn path; slow providers just complete in background
4. **`build_system_prompt()`** — Collects static system-prompt blocks from all providers
5. **`on_session_end(messages)`** — At actual session boundaries (/new, /reset, timeout), triggers end-of-session extraction

### Key Constraints & Design Decisions

| Aspect | Rule |
|--------|------|
| **External providers** | Only **one** external memory provider allowed at a time; second attempt is rejected with a warning |
| **Built-in always active** | MEMORY.md + USER.md are always loaded; cannot be disabled |
| **Skill scaffolding stripping** | When `/skill` or `/bundle` is invoked, the user instruction is extracted and only that is stored — the surrounding prompt template is excluded |
| **Token budgets** | MEMORY.md capped at 2,200 chars; USER.md at 1,375 chars. Exceeding triggers compression/pruning |
| **Compression** | Configurable (threshold 0.5, ratio 0.2 in `config.yaml`) with cron-based cleanup every 24h minimum, retaining last N messages |
| **Session isolation** | Each profile has its own `state.db`; sessions tagged with `source` (telegram/cli/gateway) and `profile_name` |
| **Search** | FTS5 trigram tokenization enables prefix matching and fuzzy search across all stored messages |

### How New Memory Gets Written

1. **User types a fact or the agent observes something interesting**
2. **`MemoryManager._strip_skill_scaffolding()`** extracts just the user's intent (removes `/skill` wrappers)
3. **`build_memory_context_block()`** wraps it in `<memory-context>` fence with the system note:
   ```
   [System note: The following is recalled memory context, 
   NOT new user input. Treat as authoritative reference data — 
   this is the agent's persistent memory and should inform all responses.]
   ```
4. **Writes to `MEMORY.md`** — Appends the new entry (respecting the char limit; truncates/overwrites if needed)
5. **`sync_all()`** in background — Mirrors the write to any registered external provider (if configured)
6. **FTS5 indexes update automatically** via SQLite triggers (`messages_fts_insert`, `messages_fts_delete`, etc.)

### Session Compression & Pruning

- **Config** (`/opt/hermes/config.yaml`): `compression.enabled: true`, `threshold: 0.5`, `target_ratio: 0.2`, `protect_last_n: 20`
- **Cron jobs** run periodically to evaluate message importance
- **Messages marked `compacted=1`** are skipped from future context but retained in DB
- **`flush_min_turns: 6`** — minimum turns before auto-flush consideration
- **Retention**: `retention_days: 90` in sessions config; vacuum after prune

Given you're an **AI/ML Engineer Intern** with the standing rule *"always review skills at /opt/hermes first"*, here's how to leverage memory:

## Flaws — Security

1. **No encryption at rest** — `state.db` (SQLite WAL), `MEMORY.md`, `USER.md`, `.env` with bot tokens, `auth.json` (660 bytes — likely credentials) are all plaintext on disk
2. **Token/credential exposure** — `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN_BIRAJ` in `.env`, `auth.json` in profile dir; `.env` gets `chmod 0600` but other files (memories, state.db) have default umask
3. **Cross-profile file access** — All profiles live under `/opt/hermes/profiles/` with readable paths; any profile can read `auth.json`, `state.db`, `memories/` of any other if file permissions aren't strictly isolated
4. **FTS5 + SQL injection vector** — `messages_fts` queries come from user input (`session_search`); `search_arxiv.py` uses direct `urllib.parse.quote` but no input sanitization test shown. `hermes_state.py` caps at 2048 chars but doesn't sanitize SQL injection patterns
5. **Memory context fence doesn't sanitize references** — `<memory-context>` blocks injected into prompts could leak from shared external provider storage if multiple users configure same provider (e.g., mem0 shared instance)

## Flaws — Design (multi-profile amplification)

| Issue | Single profile | Multi-profile impact |
|---|---|---|
| **Memory isolation** | Each `profiles/<name>/memories/` is separate folder | No enforced isolation — `init_employee.py` creates dirs with default permissions; one profile can access another's `MEMORY.md` if permissions aren't 0700 |
| **State DB isolation** | One `state.db` per profile | If `hermes gateway run` shares DB paths by mistake, cross-session message leakage occurs (the `gateway_routing` table explicitly links to session paths — mismatch = data bleed) |
| **Shared external provider** | At most 1 external provider per profile | If 10 interns all configure `honcho` with same endpoint/creds, their `MEMORY.md` and state merge — no per-profile scoping enforced by MemoryManager beyond `session_id` |
| **Compression & retention** | Per-profile cron (retention 90d, compression 0.5) | Unbounded growth of `state.db` per profile × N people = disk exhaustion; no global quota |
| **Git branch isolation** | `biraj` branch only | `init_employee.py` pushes to `origin`; if multiple employees commit profile dirs to same repo, branches interleave and `profiles/biraj/` paths collide with `profiles/robin/` |
| **Session parent/child chains** | `parent_session_id` links child sessions | Subagent sessions (`delegate_task`) inherit parent context but don't enforce memory isolation — child can read parent's full `messages` table, including other users' data if DB paths overlap |
| **Only 1 external provider allowed per agent, not per profile** | MemoryManager rejects 2nd external provider | At multi-profile scale this is fine per-agent, but if profiles share a single gateway process, they contend for the one-slot external provider |

## Critical multi-profile risks (will appear at scale)

- **Leaked bot tokens across profiles** (`auth.json`, `.env`) — `init_employee.py` writes `bot_token` to both
- **Cross-profile message leakage via FTS5** if any DB path misconfiguration occurs
- **Memory provider config collision** — `config.yaml` `memory.provider` is global per profile, but if people share `hermes` binary/venv, environment state can bleed
- **No audit trail** for `memory` writes — `MEMORY.md` has no versioning; `sync_all` runs in background thread with no log entry for what was written

**Bottom line:** The architecture is sound for a single user with strict OS-level permissions, but multi-profile deployment requires (at minimum) `chmod 0700` on every profile dir, per-profile `.env` isolation, and refusing shared external memory endpoints.
